stimulus.text: “After one year from the ratification of this article the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors within, the importation thereof into, or the exportation thereof from the United States and all territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof for beverage purposes is hereby prohibited.” — Eighteenth Amendment, Section 1, ratified 1919; in effect January 17, 1920.
stimulus.source_note: Eighteenth Amendment, Section 1. Verbatim excerpt, public domain (U.S. Constitution).

source: original; stimulus verbatim from the Eighteenth Amendment, Section 1, public domain
stem: The amendment bans the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcohol but says nothing about drinking it. That gap best helps explain why

options.text: Prohibition ended within a single short year
options.misconception: Prohibition lasted almost fourteen years, until repeal in 1933. It did not end in a single year.

options.text: temperance groups stopped supporting the law entirely
options.misconception: Temperance groups kept defending Prohibition. The law failed in the cities, not in their meeting halls.

options.text: Congress never passed an enforcement law at all
options.misconception: Congress did pass one: the Volstead Act of 1919, over President Wilson's veto. Enforcement existed; it failed.

options.text: people kept drinking while the trade went underground

rationales.A: Prohibition lasted almost fourteen years, until repeal in 1933. It did not end in a single year.
rationales.B: Temperance groups kept defending Prohibition. The law failed in the cities, not in their meeting halls.
rationales.C: Congress did pass one: the Volstead Act of 1919, over President Wilson's veto. Enforcement existed; it failed.
rationales.D: Background from the books: drinking itself was never banned, so the demand stayed while the legal supply vanished. Bootleggers and speakeasies filled the gap, and organized crime grew rich on it.
rationales.general:
1. Note what the amendment bans: making, selling, and moving alcohol.
2. Note what it leaves alone: drinking it.
3. Ask what happens when demand stays and legal supply ends: an illegal supply appears.
4. Name that supply. Background: bootleggers and speakeasies filled the gap, and organized crime grew rich on it.
Remember: a ban on supply that leaves demand alone creates a black market, not an end to use.
